background.definition: Myalgic encephalitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a clinical diagnosis for a condition marked by fatigue lasting for at least 6 months for which other medical diagnoses have been excluded. Diagnostic criteria are summarized in

list.listitem: Estimates of prevalence of ME/CFS in the general population range from under 0.8% to over 2.2%.
Prevalence rates appear to be roughly comparable in white and black populations.
Women are 3 to 4 times as likely to be affected as men.
Prevalence is highest in the sixth decade of life.
$9 billion lost productivity per year in the US.
$20,000 lost per person with ME/CFS.
The cause or causes of ME/CFS remain unknown.
Conditions that have been proposed to trigger the development of ME/CFS include viral infection or other transient traumatic conditions, stress, and toxins.
Unclear but likely multifactorial.
Impaired generation and utilization of ATP and other problems with energy metabolism have been identified.

No single infectious agent has been found to be associated with chronic fatigue, despite investigation of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), enterovirus, rubella, Candida albicans, and others. A prospective study of 20 patients with ME/CFS and 10 control patients failed to show ongoing or reactivated EBV, herpesvirus-6, or cytomegalovirus infection in patients with ME/CFS.
Onset of ME/CFS following COVID-19 infection has been widely reported ("long COVID").
Immune dysfunction has also been proposed. Changes in cytokines have been noted comparing patients with ME/CFS and controls possibly indicating immune activation and inflammation.

In general, although patients with ME/CFS may differ from the remainder of the population by some measurements (eg, cortisol levels or T-cell function), individual patient characteristics vary widely. No single factor has yet been identified to explain symptoms in all patients.
Look for other explanations for persistent fatigue (eg, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia, hypothyroidism, multiple sclerosis). C
A diagnosis of depression does not exclude ME/CFS. C
National Academy of Medicine diagnostic criteria are summarized in .

Differential.Differential_Features: May have serologic tumor markers, weight loss, abnormal imaging studies
Including CKD, DM, hypercortisolism, hypo or hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypercalcemia. Abnormal hormone levels if clinically suspected.
More likely to snore, be overweight; abnormal sleep study
Abnormal serology for Hepatitis B or C, Lyme disease, HIV.
Celiac disease, cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, small intestine bacterial overgrowth. If suspected metabolic panel, liver USN, CRP, tissue transglutaminase, endoscopy.
Anemia, iron overload. CBC with ferritin
ME/CFS more likely to have sore throat, headaches, postexertional malaise
Can include Gulf war syndrome, heavy metals, mold. Chest radiography, lead levels, history may be helpful.
Fluctuating weakness, diplopia. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

list.listitem: The National Academy of Medicine criteria for ME/CFS are summarized in
Ask patients who present with fatigue about the duration of symptoms and nonfatigue diagnostic criteria.
A preceding infection such as mononucleosis, encephalitis, or COVID-19 may be reported.

Post-exertional fatigue is the most important feature that distinguishes ME/CFS from other diagnoses that cause fatigue. This is characterized by a prolonged worsening of symptoms after an increase in activity that had been tolerated previously. Patients may describe it as a "relapse" or "crash". It can be triggered by cognitive and emotional stressors as well as physical.

Most common symptoms are unrefreshing sleep (98% in one study), muscle pain (about 90%), postexertional fatigue or malaise (about 80%), joint pain (about 80%), information processing, memory or concentration problems (about 80%), and headaches (60%).
There are no typical physical examination findings for patients with ME/CFS.
Evaluate for alternative diagnoses with a careful history and physical examination and basic laboratory testing as summarized below.
ME/CFS is not a psychological disorder and patients, who often have severe and disabling symptoms, are not lazy or malingering.

Useful questions can include: Duration and pattern of fatigue, and triggers. Factors that relieve and exacerbate fatigue Current level of function compared with previous; impact on work, school, other responsibilities. How do you feel after activity, and how much activity is required to feel ill or fatigued? Any sleep problems (amount, difficulty, quality, feeling rested) Cognitive symptoms: able to read, watch a film, participate in a conversation, multitask? Orthostatic symptoms?

Tests should be directed toward confirming or excluding other diagnostic possibilities. Studies of the prevalence of ME/CFS have used a panel of common laboratory tests, including CBC, complete metabolic profile, TSH, sedimentation rate or CRP, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor, transferrin, HIV test, and UA.

In clinical practice, no additional tests, including laboratory tests or neuroimaging studies, can be recommended for the specific purpose of diagnosing ME/CFS. In one study, there were no differences in 2 brain MRIs 1 year apart between patients with ME/CFS (N = 18) and controls (N = 9).

In one retrospective study (N = 92 after excluding 26 patients with sleep apnea or restless leg syndrome), 80% of patients with fibromyalgia and CFS had sleep abnormalities on multiple sleep latency testing (eg, hypersomnia and fragmented sleep).
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
See for a symptom-driven approach to treatment. Focus initially on the most severe symptoms.
Treatment begins with an accurate diagnosis of ME/CFS and validation of the patient's symptoms and concerns. The mantra "Stop, rest, pace" is recommended to support pacing of activity.C
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is not harmful and may assist with some aspects of ME/CFS but does not improve fatigue. C
Schedule regular visits with the patient and offer telemedicine visits as an option. C
Tricyclic antidepressants in a low dose are often used for symptomatic relief. C
Treatment should be individualized to the patient's primary symptoms. See for a summary of pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic treatments by symptoms.
Steroids (eg, hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone) and ondansetron (a 5-hydroxytryptakine receptor antoagonist) have not been shown to be helpful.
Evidence regarding antiviral drugs is inconclusive and largely negative.
If using medications for symptom relief, note that people with ME/CFS are often sensitive to side effects and may achieve therapeutic benefit at lower-than-usual doses.
A systematic review found no good evidence regarding treatment of ME/CFS associated anxiety and depression in children and adolescents.
Mirtazapine following CBT was more beneficial than CBT alone in a randomized trial.
A small trial found increases in peak VO2 with pyridostigmine compared with placebo. Additional trials are underway, including combining it with naltrexone and of naltrexone alone.
No consistent benefit seen for supplements or homeopathy.
Use of essential fatty acids, liver extracts, pollen extracts, medicinal mushrooms, and a low-sugar, low-yeast diet have been investigated with inconsistent or disappointing results.
One small series with 32 magnesium-deficient adults found a benefit to supplementation.
There is insufficient evidence to support acupuncture, moxibustion, or Chinese herbal therapies.
Nonpharmacologic treatments for symptoms of ME/CFS is shown in

Patients should be taught to pace their activity and stay within their energy capacity. The phrase "Stop, rest, pace" should be taught to support pacing. This is to help patients stay within their energy envelope and avoid post-exertional malaise "crashes".

Exercise therapy has been thought to improve physical function and reduce fatigue at 12 weeks. However, a systematic review concluded that benefits of physical therapy disappear when more precise case definitions, more objective outcome measures, and longer follow-up are used in studies.

CBT appears to improve physical functioning (NNT = 2) and is well tolerated by most patients in the short-term; findings at follow-up are heterogeneous and inconsistent.This was also found in a mixed methods systematic review, which emphasized the potential benefit of group CBT. Authors of a review paper refute success claims of CBT and state that some patients report adverse effects. A meta-analysis of three RCTs found similar rates of symptom deterioration for patients with CFS randomized to CBT and control groups. Lower cortisol levels in one study predicted poorer response to CBT in patients with CFS.
Supportive listening by trained nurse therapists was not helpful.
A systematic review found low quality evidence from small studies supporting various mind-body interventions.
Without treatment, improvement is common but full recovery is rare. B
CFS has a variable course. Some people become disabled; some require a change to their job; still others resume full activities.

Even without treatment, many patients with CSF (average 39% over studies reviewed) report meaningful improvement in their symptoms over time; complete recovery is also seen in about 7%. In a study of adolescents (N = 54) with CFS, about half reported nearly complete improvement at 2 years, the remainder reported no improvement.
Studies conducted in the primary care setting were associated with higher rates of improvement than those conducted in specialty practices.
Better outcome was associated with milder fatigue at presentation. In one follow-up study, patients with both fibromyalgia and CFS were less likely to improve at 2 years.
About 25% of patients are able to work, while 10% to 25% are home or bed bound.
Patients who are diagnosed sooner (within 2 years of symptom onset) are more likely to have improved outcomes.
Alternate diagnostic criteria have been proposed for use in children, requiring only 3 months of fatigue rather than 6.

algorithm.title: Algorithm for the Diagnosis of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.

cell.label: Fatigue, unrelieved by rest, for at least 6 months?
Does not meet definition of CFS.

At least four of the following are present: • Substantial impairment in short-term memory or concentration • Sore throat • Tender lymph nodes • Muscle pain • Multijoint pain without swelling or redness • Headaches of a new type, pattern, or severity • Unrefreshing sleep • Postexertional malaise lasting for more than 24 h that started with or after the fatigue?
Other medical explanation (eg, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea)?
Relapse of preexisting condition (eg, malignancy, hepatitis)?

Current or prior diagnosis of: • Major depressive disorder with psychotic or melancholic features • Bipolar affective disorders • Schizophrenia of any subtype • Delusional disorders of any subtype • Dementias of any subtype • Anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa.
Alcohol/substance abuse at any time after 2 y before onset of fatigue?

tr.td: Post-exertional malaise
Profound fatigue with substantially decrease in ability to engage in usual activity or function

Lightheadedness, nausea, fatigue, palpitations, or syncope with prolonged standing
GI or GU symptoms, hypersensitivity to stiimuli, or impaired immune function
Flu-like symptoms, association with a previous infection such as mono or COVID-19, or respiratory problems.
